html:
The siege of Málaga lasted from May to August 1487 at Málaga, on the south coast of Spain. The armies of Ferdinand and Isabella took the city from the Muslim Emirate of Granada.

Málaga was the emirate's second city and its main port, the door through which help could come from North Africa. In the Granada War, Ferdinand and Isabella were taking the emirate apart town by town, and Granada itself was split by a civil war between rival emirs. Málaga had strong walls and two castles. Its garrison of North African soldiers under Hamet el Zegrí refused all terms. The Christian army ringed the city with trenches and guns, and a fleet closed the sea. The fighting was hard for more than three months. A field hospital with wagons for the wounded was set up, often called the first ambulances. Hunger ended it: the townspeople forced a surrender in August.

Because the city had resisted, Ferdinand gave no terms. Almost all of its people, perhaps 11,000 to 15,000, were enslaved or held for ransom. The loss cut Granada off from the sea, and the capital fell in 1492, ending the Reconquista.
